item.title: The Last Light on the Sentiero Azzurro
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: On the Trail When the day-trippers have gone and the trail belongs to evening The Last Light on the Sentiero Azzurro Golden Hour Most people walk the Sentiero Azzurro in the morning. They’re up early, beating the heat and the crowds, which makes sense if you’re trying to cover all five villages in a day. […]
item.content:encoded:
On the Trail

When the day-trippers have gone and the trail belongs to evening

The Last Light on the Sentiero Azzurro

Golden Hour

Most people walk the Sentiero Azzurro in the morning. They’re up early, beating the heat and the crowds, which makes sense if you’re trying to cover all five villages in a day. But they miss this—the hour when the trail exhales, when the limestone path still holds the day’s warmth under your feet and the sea below turns from tourist-brochure blue to something deeper, more private.

I’m not saying you should skip the morning walk. The light is beautiful then too, crisp and clear, good for photographs. But if you want to understand why people have been walking this coastline for centuries, why the muleteers and the farmers and the smugglers all took this same route, you need to see it at the end of the day.

There’s a particular quality to the light here between six and seven in the evening—honey-thick and slanting, the kind that makes ordinary stone walls look like they’re holding secrets.

The climb out of Vernazza is the hardest part—always has been. Three hundred steps, though I’ve never counted them myself. You can still see the original stone steps laid centuries ago, worn smooth in the middle where generations of feet found the same comfortable groove. The tourists who started at dawn are long gone. The shops are closing. Someone is watering the lemon trees in their terraced garden below, and the smell of it rises up with the basil and the salt.

Your legs complain. Let them. By the time you reach the first real viewpoint—you’ll know it when you see it—your breathing has found its rhythm and the village has dropped away behind you.

This is where the trail really begins, where it stops being about getting from one village to another and becomes about the walking itself. The path narrows, pressed between the hillside and the drop to the sea. On your left, the terraces climb up in their ancient geometry—the muretti a secco, dry stone walls that have held these slopes in place for eight hundred years. Someone is still farming up there. You can see the stakes for the vines, the silver-green leaves of olive trees that were old when your grandparents were born.

The light is changing now, getting richer. It catches in the wild fennel growing between the stones, turns the agave flowers into torches. Below, the water is doing that thing it does in the evening, layering itself into bands of color—pale aquamarine close to shore where you can see the rocks, then green, then blue, then that deep almost-purple that means depth, real depth, the kind where the bottom drops away to nothing.

There’s a hidden bay below the path, just past the halfway point to Corniglia. You won’t find it on any map worth mentioning, and I’m not going to tell you exactly where it is—some things you find yourself or you don’t find at all. But you’ll hear it first, the particular sound of water moving over smooth stones, different from the open-sea sound you’ve been hearing. If you look carefully through the scrub oak and the mastic, you might catch the white flash of surf on rocks, a small crescent of beach that no one has touched since this morning, maybe longer.

My nonna used to say that walking this path in the evening meant you could smell what everyone was making for dinner—the garlic hitting hot olive oil in a hundred different kitchens, the particular sharpness of anchovies being rinsed of their salt, the green smell of basil being torn by hand. The wind carries it up from the villages on both sides. On Thursdays you might catch the wood smoke from the bakery ovens being fired up for tomorrow’s focaccia. In October, someone is always making passata, and the whole coast smells like tomatoes being put up for winter.

The train passes below, the evening run heading toward La Spezia. You hear the horn first, then see the silver flash moving between the tunnels. The sound echoes up the rock face, changes pitch in the distance. When I was small, I used to time my walks to the trains, using them the way other people use a watch. The 18:42 meant you had half an hour of good light left. The 19:17 meant you’d better know the path well, because the shadows were getting serious.

I walked this section last Tuesday evening, just as the light was starting to go amber. A couple from Milano had the same idea—we passed each other twice, going slow, not talking much. At the Corniglia end, where the path spills out into the village, we nodded at each other, the way you do when you’ve shared something without having to explain it. They got it. That hour belongs to people who understand that getting there isn’t really the point.

Giulia Rossi

Local Editor

The last section into Corniglia is different. The path widens, becomes more of a proper trail. You’re higher now, and the views open up—you can see back to Vernazza, forward to Manarola, the whole sweep of coast laid out like a promise. The light is horizontal now, that last-gasp golden that photographers wait hours for. It makes everything look like it’s been dipped in honey—the stone, the vegetation, even your own hands when you look at them.

By the time you reach the village, the light is starting to fail. The street lamps are coming on. Someone is setting tables at the restaurant in the piazza, and the church bells ring for evening Mass, the way they have for five hundred years. You’re tired—the good kind of tired, the kind that comes from using your body the way it was meant to be used. Your legs will remember this tomorrow, especially those first steps out of Vernazza.

But for now, find a seat at one of the small bars in the upper village. Order something cold. Watch the sky do its final performance over the water—rose, then orange, then that particular violet that means the day is finished. The trail is dark now. The people who walked it this morning are already at dinner, posting their photos, planning tomorrow’s itinerary. They saw the Sentiero Azzurro in daylight, which is fine, which is good. But you saw it in the last light. And that makes all the difference.

Explore the Sentiero Azzurro
More Trail Stories

Practical Notes

The evening walk requires some preparation. Bring a headlamp—the last section will be in twilight, and the path, while well-maintained, has some uneven spots. The trail officially closes at sunset, but locals have walked it at dusk for generations. Use your judgment and your common sense.

Start from Vernazza between 5:30 and 6:00 PM in summer, earlier in spring and fall. The walk to Corniglia takes about 90 minutes at an evening pace—slower than your morning speed, and that’s the point. You’re not racing daylight; you’re watching it change.

Water, yes. Snacks, maybe. But leave the photography ambitions for another time. This walk is about being present, about noticing how the color of the water changes minute by minute, about hearing the train and the dinner sounds and your own breathing. The images you take home from this one will be in your head, which is where the best ones belong anyway.

Walking at Golden Hour

item.title: La guida definitiva alle migliori spiagge delle Cinque Terre
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Dalle spiagge sabbiose di Monterosso alle calette nascoste di Riomaggiore, esploriamo i luoghi piu belli per nuotare nella Riviera Ligure.
item.content:encoded:
Nata e cresciuta a Riomaggiore, Giulia ha passato la vita ad esplorare gli angoli nascosti delle Cinque Terre. E la caporedattrice di The Dispatch e guida locale certificata.

Giulia Rossi

Guide

L’aria salmastra delle Cinque Terre e diversa. Porta con se il profumo del timo selvatico delle colline e quello della pietra antica dei borghi. Ma soprattutto, porta la promessa del mare. Per chi sa dove cercare, i cinque borghi offrono alcune delle esperienze di nuoto piu spettacolari del Mediterraneo.

Level 2

Il santuario di sabbia: Monterosso al Mare

Monterosso e l’unico borgo con una vera spiaggia di sabbia. Fegina, la parte piu moderna del paese, vanta una lunga distesa di sabbia dorata e acqua turchese cristallina. E il luogo perfetto per le famiglie e per chi preferisce un’esperienza balneare tradizionale con ombrelloni e lettini.

Giulia Rossi, Esperta locale

Se vuoi nuotare come un locale, devi abbracciare gli scogli. L’acqua migliore non e dove c’e la sabbia, ma dove le scogliere incontrano il blu profondo.

Level 2

La caletta nascosta: Fossola a Riomaggiore

Per chi e disposto a camminare un po’ di piu, la spiaggia di Fossola a Riomaggiore offre un’esperienza piu selvaggia. Questa spiaggia di ciottoli e nascosta dietro il porto e richiede di percorrere un sentiero stretto lungo la scogliera. La ricompensa? Acqua smeraldo profonda e un senso di isolamento difficile da trovare nel pieno dell’estate.

Level 2

Consigli pratici per i nuotatori

La maggior parte delle spiagge e di ciottoli o scogli. Proteggete i piedi dalle pietre taglienti e dai ricci di mare.

Indossate le scarpette da scoglio

Il momento migliore per nuotare e prima delle 10 del mattino, quando l’acqua e calma e la folla e ancora a colazione.

Andate presto

Anche un leggero moto ondoso puo rendere pericoloso entrare e uscire dalle calette rocciose. Rispettate sempre il mare.

Controllate lo stato del mare

item.title: 5 gelaterie nascoste da provare assolutamente
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Evitate le trappole per turisti e scoprite i veri tesori. I nostri esperti locali rivelano dove trovare il gelato artigianale piu cremoso nei cinque borghi.
item.content:encoded:
Marco e uno scrittore gastronomico e storico della cucina che ha trascorso decenni a documentare le ricette tradizionali della Liguria. E convinto che i piatti migliori siano spesso i piu semplici.

Marco Bianchi

Gastronomia

In una regione dove i turisti affollano le vetrine piu visibili, il gelato davvero straordinario spesso si nasconde in bella vista – in fondo a un vicolo stretto, oltre una porta che solo i locali conoscono a memoria, o in un borgo che non compare in cima a nessun itinerario. Ecco le cinque gelaterie che hanno conquistato la nostra devozione.

Level 2

1. Gelateria Centrale, Riomaggiore

Nascosta in un angolo di Via Colombo che la maggior parte dei visitatori ignora, la Gelateria Centrale prepara tutto fresco ogni mattina. Il limone e fatto con i limoni delle terrazze sopra il paese, e si puo assaporare l’aria salmastra in ogni morso. Chiedete la crema di limone – non e in vetrina, ma la preparano volentieri se chiedete con garbo.

Marco Bianchi

Il miglior gelato delle Cinque Terre non e questione di gusti esotici. E assaporare il luogo stesso – i limoni delle terrazze, le nocciole delle colline, la semplicita che nasce dal fare una cosa sola alla perfezione.

Level 2

2. Il Porticciolo Gelateria, Manarola

Questo minuscolo locale vicino al porto serve quello che potrebbe essere il miglior gelato al pistacchio di tutta la costa ligure. Il proprietario si rifornisce di pistacchi direttamente da Bronte, in Sicilia, e si sente la differenza. La consistenza e incredibilmente cremosa, il colore e naturalmente verde (non il verde fosforescente degli aromi artificiali), e il gusto persiste a lungo dopo che il cono e finito.

Level 2

3. Gelateria 5 Terre, Monterosso

Sebbene Monterosso non manchi certo di opzioni per il gelato, questa bottega a conduzione familiare ai margini del centro storico supera costantemente la concorrenza. La loro specialita e il gusto Sciacchetra – gelato fatto con il vino passito locale. E dolce, complesso e assolutamente unico di questo tratto di costa.

Level 2

4. Alberto Gelateria, Vernazza

Alberto prepara gelato a Vernazza da oltre quarant’anni. La sua bottega e facile da perdere – nessuna insegna appariscente, solo una piccola porta che si apre sulla piazza. Provate la nocciola, fatta con le noci delle colline piemontesi. Vale la pena pagare l’euro in piu per una doppia pallina.

Level 2

5. Il posto segreto, Corniglia

Questo non ve lo nominiamo – se lo trovate, capirete perche. E in cima al paese, oltre la piazza principale, in un edificio che non sembra affatto una gelateria. La donna che lo gestisce prepara solo tre gusti al giorno, in base a cio che e fresco. Fidatevi del suo giudizio.

Osservate come viene servito. Se usano una spatola e il gelato si piega morbidamente, e quello vero. Se viene scavato come il gelato industriale, andate oltre.

Il test della spatola

Il miglior gelato viene preparato fresco ogni mattina. Andate prima delle 15 per texture e sapore ottimali.

Il momento giusto

Guida fotografica a Manarola al tramonto

Cercate colori naturali – il verde fosforescente e un segnale d’allarme.

item.title: Le guide ultime des plus belles plages des Cinque Terre
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Des plages de sable de Monterosso aux criques rocheuses secretes de Riomaggiore, decouvrez les plus beaux endroits pour se baigner sur la Riviera italienne.
item.content:encoded:
Nee et elevee a Riomaggiore, Giulia a consacre sa vie a explorer les recoins secrets des Cinque Terre. Elle est redactrice en chef de The Dispatch et guide locale certifiee.

Giulia Rossi

Guides

L’air sale des Cinque Terre est different. Il porte le parfum du thym sauvage des collines et la senteur de la pierre ancestrale des villages. Mais surtout, il porte la promesse de la mer. Pour ceux qui savent ou chercher, les cinq villages offrent certaines des experiences de baignade les plus spectaculaires de la Mediterranee.

Level 2

Le sanctuaire de sable : Monterosso al Mare

Monterosso est le seul village disposant d’une veritable plage de sable. Fegina, la partie moderne de la ville, offre une longue etendue de sable dore et d’eau turquoise cristalline. C’est l’endroit ideal pour les familles et ceux qui preferent une experience balneaire traditionnelle avec parasols et transats.

Giulia Rossi, Experte locale

Si vous voulez nager comme un local, il faut apprivoiser les rochers. La meilleure eau n’est pas la ou il y a du sable, mais la ou les falaises rencontrent le bleu profond.

Level 2

La crique secrete : Fossola a Riomaggiore

Pour ceux qui acceptent de marcher un peu plus, la plage de Fossola a Riomaggiore offre une experience plus sauvage. Cette plage de galets est nichee derriere le port et necessite d’emprunter un etroit sentier le long de la falaise. La recompense ? Une eau emeraude profonde et un sentiment d’isolement rare en plein ete.

Level 2

Conseils pratiques pour les baigneurs

La plupart des plages sont de galets ou rocheuses. Protegez vos pieds des pierres coupantes et des oursins.

Portez des chaussures aquatiques

La meilleure baignade est avant 10h, quand l’eau est calme et que la foule est encore au petit-dejeuner.

Partez tot

Meme une legere houle peut rendre l’entree et la sortie des criques rocheuses dangereuses. Respectez toujours la mer.

Verifiez l’etat de la mer

15 octobre 2023

8 min de lecture

Le matin tot est le meilleur moment pour une eau calme.

item.title: 5 gelaterias cachees a decouvrir absolument
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Evitez les pieges a touristes et decouvrez les vraies pepites. Nos experts locaux revelent ou trouver les glaces artisanales les plus onctueuses des cinq villages.
item.content:encoded:
Marco est un critique gastronomique et historien culinaire qui a consacre des decennies a documenter les recettes traditionnelles de la Ligurie. Il est convaincu que les meilleurs repas sont souvent les plus simples.

Marco Bianchi

Gastronomie

Dans une region ou les touristes affluent vers les vitrines les plus visibles, les glaces vraiment remarquables se cachent souvent a la vue de tous – au fond d’une ruelle etroite, derriere une porte que seuls les habitants connaissent par coeur, ou dans un village qui ne figure pas en tete des itineraires. Voici les cinq gelaterias qui ont gagne notre devotion.

Level 2

1. Gelateria Centrale, Riomaggiore

Nichee dans un coin de la Via Colombo que la plupart des visiteurs depassent sans s’arreter, la Gelateria Centrale prepare tout frais chaque matin. Le citron (limone) est fait avec des citrons des terrasses au-dessus du village, et on peut gouter l’air marin a chaque bouchee. Demandez la crema di limone – elle n’est pas en vitrine, mais ils la prepareront si vous demandez gentiment.

Marco Bianchi

La meilleure glace des Cinque Terre n’est pas une question de saveurs exotiques. C’est gouter le lieu lui-meme – les citrons des terrasses, les noisettes des collines, la simplicite qui vient de faire parfaitement une seule chose.

Level 2

2. Il Porticciolo Gelateria, Manarola

Ce minuscule etablissement pres du port sert peut-etre la meilleure glace a la pistache de toute la cote ligure. Le proprietaire s’approvisionne directement a Bronte, en Sicile, et on sent la difference. La texture est incroyablement onctueuse, la couleur est naturellement verte (pas le vert fluo des aromes artificiels), et le gout persiste longtemps apres la derniere bouchee.

Level 2

3. Gelateria 5 Terre, Monterosso

Bien que Monterosso ne manque pas d’options de glaces, cette boutique familiale en bordure de la vieille ville surpasse constamment ses concurrents. Leur specialite est le parfum Sciacchetra – une glace elaboree avec le vin de dessert local. Elle est douce, complexe et absolument unique a cette partie de la cote.

Level 2

4. Alberto Gelateria, Vernazza

Alberto fait des glaces a Vernazza depuis plus de quarante ans. Sa boutique est facile a manquer – pas d’enseigne tape-a-l’oeil, juste une petite porte donnant sur la place. Essayez la nocciola (noisette), faite avec des noix des collines du Piemont. L’euro supplementaire pour une double boule en vaut la peine.

Level 2

5. L’adresse secrete, Corniglia

Nous n’allons pas nommer celui-ci – si vous le trouvez, vous comprendrez pourquoi. C’est en haut du village, apres la place principale, dans un batiment qui ne ressemble pas du tout a une gelateria. La femme qui le tient ne prepare que trois parfums chaque jour, selon ce qui est frais. Faites confiance a son jugement.

Observez comment le serveur fait les portions. S’il utilise une spatule et que la glace se plie doucement, c’est la vraie affaire. Si elle est servie comme une boule de creme glacee, passez votre chemin.

Le test de la spatule

Le meilleur gelato est prepare frais chaque matin. Passez avant 15h pour une texture et une saveur optimales.

Le timing compte

14 octobre 2023

item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Cinque Terre’s Best Beaches
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: From the sandy shores of Monterosso to the hidden rocky coves of Riomaggiore, we explore the most pristine swimming spots in the Italian Riviera.
item.content:encoded:
Born and raised in Riomaggiore, Giulia has spent her life exploring the hidden corners of the Cinque Terre. She is the lead editor of The Dispatch and a certified local guide.

Giulia Rossi

Guides

The salt air in Cinque Terre is different. It carries the scent of wild thyme from the hills and the ancient stone of the villages. But most importantly, it carries the promise of the sea. For those who know where to look, the five villages offer some of the most spectacular swimming experiences in the Mediterranean.

Level 2

The Sandy Sanctuary: Monterosso al Mare

Monterosso is the only village with a proper sandy beach. Fegina, the newer part of town, boasts a long stretch of golden sand and crystal-clear turquoise water. It’s the perfect spot for families and those who prefer a more traditional beach experience with umbrellas and sunbeds.

Giulia Rossi, Local Expert

If you want to swim like a local, you have to embrace the rocks. The best water isn’t where the sand is; it’s where the cliffs meet the deep blue.

Level 2

The Hidden Cove: Riomaggiore’s Fossola

For those willing to walk a bit further, Fossola beach in Riomaggiore offers a wilder experience. This pebble beach is tucked behind the harbor and requires navigating a narrow path along the cliffside. The reward? Deep, emerald water and a sense of isolation that’s hard to find in the peak of summer.

Level 2

Practical Tips for Swimmers

Most beaches are pebbly or rocky. Protect your feet from sharp stones and sea urchins.

Wear Water Shoes

The best swimming is before 10 AM when the water is calm and the crowds are still at breakfast.

Go Early

Even a slight swell can make getting in and out of rocky coves dangerous. Always respect the sea.

Check the Sea State

item.title: 5 Hidden Gelaterias You Need to Try
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Skip the tourist traps and find the real deal. Our local experts reveal where to find the creamiest artisanal gelato in the five villages.
item.content:encoded:
Marco is a food writer and culinary historian who has spent decades documenting the traditional recipes of Liguria. He believes the best meals are often the simplest.

Marco Bianchi

Food

In a region where tourists flock to the most visible storefronts, the truly remarkable gelato often hides in plain sight-down a narrow alley, through a doorway that locals know by heart, or in a village that doesn’t make the top of anyone’s itinerary. Here are the five gelaterias that have earned our devotion.

Level 2

1. Gelateria Centrale, Riomaggiore

Tucked into a corner of Via Colombo that most visitors walk right past, Gelateria Centrale makes everything fresh each morning. The lemon (limone) here is made with lemons from the terraces above the village, and you can taste the salt air in every bite. Ask for the crema di limone-it’s not on the display, but they’ll make it if you ask nicely.

Marco Bianchi

The best gelato in Cinque Terre isn’t about exotic flavors. It’s about tasting the place itself-the lemons from the terraces, the hazelnuts from the hills, the simplicity that comes from doing one thing perfectly.

Level 2

2. Il Porticciolo Gelateria, Manarola

This tiny spot near the harbor serves what might be the best pistachio gelato on the entire Ligurian coast. The owner sources pistachios directly from Bronte, Sicily, and you can taste the difference. The texture is impossibly creamy, the color is naturally green (not the neon green of artificial flavoring), and the taste lingers long after the cone is gone.

Level 2

3. Gelateria 5 Terre, Monterosso

While Monterosso has no shortage of gelato options, this family-run shop on the edge of the old town consistently outperforms its competitors. Their specialty is the Sciacchetra flavor-gelato made with the local dessert wine. It’s sweet, complex, and utterly unique to this stretch of coast.

Level 2

4. Alberto Gelateria, Vernazza

Alberto has been making gelato in Vernazza for over forty years. His shop is easy to miss-there’s no flashy signage, just a small doorway that opens onto the piazza. Try the nocciola (hazelnut), made with nuts from the Piedmont hills. It’s worth the extra euro for a double scoop.

Level 2

5. The Secret Spot, Corniglia

We’re not going to name this one-if you find it, you’ll understand why. It’s at the top of the village, past the main square, in a building that doesn’t look like a gelateria at all. The woman who runs it only makes three flavors each day, based on what’s fresh. Trust her judgment.

Watch how the server scoops. If they use a paddle (spatola) and the gelato folds softly, it’s the real deal. If it’s scooped like ice cream, keep walking.

The Spatula Test

The best gelato is made fresh each morning. Visit before 3 PM for the optimal texture and flavor.

Timing Matters

October 14, 2023

A Photographer’s Guide to Manarola at Sunset

4 min read

The best gelaterias are often hidden from the main tourist path.

Look for natural colors-bright neon is a warning sign.

Fresh gelato is made daily and runs out by evening.

item.title: Der ultimative Guide zu den schoensten Straenden der Cinque Terre
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Von den Sandstraenden Monterossos bis zu den versteckten Felsbuchten von Riomaggiore - entdecken Sie die schoensten Badestellen der italienischen Riviera.
item.content:encoded:
In Riomaggiore geboren und aufgewachsen, hat Giulia ihr Leben der Erkundung der verborgenen Winkel der Cinque Terre gewidmet. Sie ist Chefredakteurin von The Dispatch und zertifizierte Ortsfuehrerin.

Giulia Rossi

Reisefuehrer

Die salzige Luft der Cinque Terre ist anders. Sie traegt den Duft von wildem Thymian aus den Huegeln und den Geruch des uralten Steins der Doerfer. Doch vor allem traegt sie das Versprechen des Meeres. Wer weiss, wo man suchen muss, findet in den fuenf Doerfern einige der spektakulaersten Badeplaetze des Mittelmeers.

Level 2

Das Sandparadies: Monterosso al Mare

Monterosso ist das einzige Dorf mit einem richtigen Sandstrand. Fegina, der neuere Teil des Ortes, begeistert mit einem langen Streifen goldenen Sandes und kristallklarem tuerkisfarbenem Wasser. Der perfekte Ort fuer Familien und alle, die ein klassisches Stranderlebnis mit Sonnenschirmen und Liegen bevorzugen.

Giulia Rossi, Ortskundige Expertin

Wer schwimmen will wie ein Einheimischer, muss die Felsen lieben lernen. Das beste Wasser ist nicht dort, wo der Sand ist – sondern wo die Klippen auf das tiefe Blau treffen.

Level 2

Die versteckte Bucht: Fossola in Riomaggiore

Fuer alle, die bereit sind, etwas weiter zu gehen, bietet der Strand Fossola in Riomaggiore ein wilderes Erlebnis. Dieser Kieselstrand liegt versteckt hinter dem Hafen und ist ueber einen schmalen Pfad entlang der Steilkueste zu erreichen. Die Belohnung? Tiefgruenes Wasser und ein Gefuehl der Abgeschiedenheit, das mitten im Sommer schwer zu finden ist.

Level 2

Praktische Tipps fuer Schwimmer

Die meisten Straende sind steinig oder felsig. Schuetzen Sie Ihre Fuesse vor scharfen Steinen und Seeigeln.

Badeschuhe tragen

Die besten Badebedingungen herrschen vor 10 Uhr morgens, wenn das Wasser ruhig ist und die Massen noch beim Fruehstueck sitzen.

Frueh aufbrechen

Selbst leichter Wellengang kann den Ein- und Ausstieg in Felsbuchten gefaehrlich machen. Respektieren Sie immer das Meer.

Wellengang pruefen

item.title: 5 versteckte Gelaterias, die Sie unbedingt probieren muessen
item.dc:creator: admin
item.description: Meiden Sie die Touristenfallen und entdecken Sie echte Geheimtipps. Unsere Ortskenner verraten, wo Sie das cremigste handwerkliche Gelato in den fuenf Doerfern finden.
item.content:encoded:
Marco ist Gastronom und Kulinarik-Historiker, der Jahrzehnte damit verbracht hat, die traditionellen Rezepte Liguriens zu dokumentieren. Er ist ueberzeugt, dass die besten Gerichte oft die einfachsten sind.

Marco Bianchi

Kulinarik

In einer Region, in der Touristen zu den auffaelligsten Geschaeften stroemen, versteckt sich das wirklich aussergewoehnliche Gelato oft direkt vor aller Augen – in einer schmalen Gasse, hinter einer Tuer, die nur Einheimische kennen, oder in einem Dorf, das auf keiner Reiseroute ganz oben steht. Hier sind fuenf Gelaterias, die unsere Hingabe verdient haben.

Level 2

1. Gelateria Centrale, Riomaggiore

In einer Ecke der Via Colombo versteckt, an der die meisten Besucher vorbeigehen, stellt die Gelateria Centrale jeden Morgen alles frisch her. Das Zitronengelato (limone) wird hier mit Zitronen von den Terrassen oberhalb des Dorfes zubereitet – man kann die Meeresluft in jedem Bissen schmecken. Fragen Sie nach der Crema di Limone – sie steht nicht in der Auslage, aber man bereitet sie gerne zu, wenn Sie hoeflich fragen.

Marco Bianchi

Das beste Gelato der Cinque Terre handelt nicht von exotischen Aromen. Es geht darum, den Ort selbst zu schmecken – die Zitronen von den Terrassen, die Haselnuesse aus den Huegeln, die Einfachheit, die entsteht, wenn man eine Sache perfekt beherrscht.

Level 2

2. Il Porticciolo Gelateria, Manarola

Dieser winzige Laden nahe dem Hafen serviert vielleicht das beste Pistaziengelato der gesamten ligurischen Kueste. Der Besitzer bezieht seine Pistazien direkt aus Bronte auf Sizilien – und man schmeckt den Unterschied. Die Konsistenz ist unglaublich cremig, die Farbe ist natuerlich gruen (nicht das Neongruen kuenstlicher Aromen), und der Geschmack verweilt lange, nachdem die Waffel aufgegessen ist.

Level 2

3. Gelateria 5 Terre, Monterosso

Obwohl es in Monterosso keinen Mangel an Gelato-Angeboten gibt, uebertrifft dieser familiegefuehrte Laden am Rand der Altstadt seine Konkurrenten bestaendig. Ihre Spezialitaet ist das Sciacchetra-Gelato – hergestellt mit dem lokalen Dessertwein. Es ist suess, vielschichtig und einzigartig fuer diesen Kuestenabschnitt.

Level 2

4. Alberto Gelateria, Vernazza

Alberto stellt seit ueber vierzig Jahren Gelato in Vernazza her. Sein Geschaeft ist leicht zu uebersehen – kein auffaelliges Schild, nur eine kleine Tuer, die auf die Piazza fuehrt. Probieren Sie die Nocciola (Haselnuss), hergestellt mit Nuessen aus den piemontesischen Huegeln. Der zusaetzliche Euro fuer eine doppelte Kugel lohnt sich.

Level 2

5. Der Geheimtipp, Corniglia

Diesen nennen wir nicht beim Namen – wenn Sie ihn finden, werden Sie verstehen warum. Er liegt am oberen Ende des Dorfes, hinter dem Hauptplatz, in einem Gebaeude, das ueberhaupt nicht wie eine Gelateria aussieht. Die Frau, die ihn fuehrt, macht jeden Tag nur drei Sorten, je nachdem, was frisch ist. Vertrauen Sie ihrem Urteil.

Achten Sie darauf, wie das Gelato portioniert wird. Wenn ein Spachtel (Spatola) verwendet wird und sich das Gelato weich faltet, ist es echt. Wenn es wie normales Eis geschaufelt wird, gehen Sie weiter.

Der Spachtel-Test

Das beste Gelato wird jeden Morgen frisch zubereitet. Besuchen Sie die Gelateria vor 15 Uhr fuer optimale Konsistenz und Geschmack.

Der richtige Zeitpunkt

14. Oktober 2023

Ein Fotografen-Guide fuer Manarola bei Sonnenuntergang

4 Min. Lesezeit

Die besten Gelaterias sind oft abseits der Touristenpfade versteckt.

Achten Sie auf natuerliche Farben – Neonfarben sind ein Warnsignal.

Frisches Gelato wird taeglich hergestellt und ist abends oft ausverkauft.
